extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, philosophy of mind, and creative writers interested in imagination/memory theory
extracted.subtask_description: Explicating philosophical/psychological principles of association, memory, and imagination that underlie how images and ideas recall each other — material useful for critics and writers aiming to produce vivid, associative literary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: General law of association
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas having been together acquire a power of recalling each other; or every partial representation awakens the total representation of which it had been a part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as Aristotle's universal law: the mechanism of reproduction of impressions and the foundation of passive fancy and mechanical memory. Examples and paraphrases (e.g., partial impressions recalling whole impressions; Scipio → Antiochus) illustrate how one part of an impression can call up the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five occasioning causes of recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular recollections admit five agents or occasioning causes: 1st, connexion in time (simultaneous/preceding/successive); 2d, vicinity or connexion in space; 3d, interdependence or necessary connexion (cause and effect); 4th, likeness; and 5th, contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's enumeration (as explained by commentators) is given as the practical determinants for why particular thoughts recur; these serve as operative rules for constructing or analyzing associative chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contiguity/time as common condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaneity (connexion in time) is the common condition under which the various determining powers act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's note: time often underlies other associative principles (though not always the effective force). In recollection, we search from present to the time when the desired memory occurred; time ordering is a primary search strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeness/ressemblance as an associative influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Likeness, as co-ordinate with, but not always subordinate to, Time, exerts an influence per se on association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition and resemblance can operate independently to recall items (e.g., a part of A resembling part of B can evoke B). Likeness may be 'an act of recognition' and can determine which parts of an impression are recalled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and effect as associative principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdependence or necessary connexion, as cause and effect, functions as an occasioning cause of recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aquinas/Aristotle treat causation as a distinct associative influence; cause–effect relations can summon related ideas beyond mere temporal or spatial contiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast/opposition as associative principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct dissimilarity or Contrast operates as a separate principle of association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast (dissimilarity) can be an explicit trigger for recall and is treated alongside resemblance and contiguity in classical accounts (Aquinas, Aristotle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence/order principle in recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Recollection proceeds along relations: 'a causa ad effectum, ab hoc ad instrumentum, a parte ad totum,' thence to place, person, and to what ever preceded or followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle/Coleridge emphasize ordered pathways (cause→effect, part→whole, place→person) as habitual routes the mind follows in remembering; useful as a model for structuring associative progressions in prose or narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial marks/mediating links in association
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that a whole representation B have been together with a whole representation A; if only some mark of A (say m) has been associated with some mark of B, that is sufficient to call up B through A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how small overlapping features or 'marks' serve as mediators in associative chains — a useful technical account for how indirect or subtle imagery can trigger broader recollections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness determines recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever makes certain parts of a total impression more vivid or distinct will determine the mind to recall these rather than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge and commentators stress that parts rendered more vivid (by attention, context, emotional weight) will dominate associative recall; practical implication: emphasize and sharpen particular details to steer readers' recollection and imaginative response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will/attention intensify vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the will to give vividness to any object whatsoever by intensifying the attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active, voluntary attention increases the firmness of impression in memory and the vividness of mental images; in composition, deliberate focus can make imagery more memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom/habit as associative cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes sequence of ideas arises from custom; 'by once thinking of a thing, some men acquire a habit, more than others by thinking ever so often.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitual co-occurrence produces stable associative pathways (second nature). Repetition in experience or narrative can therefore create expected associative links for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination's operations (composition & decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phantasia (imagination) 'fingit, refingit, componit, devincit, dissolvit' — it invents, recomposes, composes, connects, dissolves, and separates images and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination is active, freely combining and altering impressions; but the text warns that imagination should be 'regulated by reason' so it does not unduly disturb or mislead the mind — balance creative invention with rational control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association supplies materials for all thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Association is 'that which supplies to all other faculties their objects, to all thought the elements of its Materials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a foundational principle: associative connections furnish the raw material of thought and imaginative work, so mastery of associative techniques is fundamental to composition and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distraction weakens memory
rubrics_metrics.description: By distraction of the imagination the mental impression is weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of focused attention or divided attention diminishes the strength of impressions and subsequent recall; in writing or teaching, reduce distractions to secure vivid retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward mechanical/physiological metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Hartley's hypothesis that vibrations in an oscillating ether of the nerves propagate ideas (vibrations a → m) is critiqued as unable to account for association because different causes cannot produce the same effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against accepting crude mechanical accounts of the imagination/mind; do not conflate physical motion metaphors with the qualitative distinctness of ideas — conceptual distinctions matter when theorizing imaginative processes or using metaphors in criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude place and motion from operations of thought (Aristotelian caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle 'excludes place and motion from all the operations of thought, whether representations or volitions, as attributes utterly and absurdly heterogeneous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A philosophical caution: avoid treating mental operations as if they were spatial/kinetic properties; metaphors of motion/place should be used carefully and not taken for literal explanatory models.
